lessons.title: From a C Library Call to a System Call
lessons.subtitle: Understand what happens when a program asks the operating system to do work.
lessons.summary: Trace the path from a familiar C output function to the operating-system interface beneath it.
learning_objectives: Distinguish a C library function from a kernel system-call interface.
Explain the roles of user space, a C library and the kernel.
Describe why tracing tools may show a write system call when a program uses printf.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with compiling and running a C program

blocks.title: The central idea
blocks.markdown: A library function and a system call are not the same thing. A library function may prepare, buffer or transform work before invoking an operating-system interface.

A typical hosted C program runs in user space. It can call library functions such as `printf`. The C library may format text and buffer output. When data must be sent to a file descriptor, the library can invoke the operating system's write interface. The kernel performs the privileged operation.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing an application calling a C library, which crosses the system-call boundary to the operating-system kernel.
blocks.caption: Conceptual path from application code through the C library to the kernel.

blocks.text: Compare two ways to write output

blocks.explanation: printf formats output through the C standard I/O library. write is a POSIX interface that requests writing bytes to a file descriptor. This example is POSIX-oriented and is not directly portable to every operating system. fflush ensures the stdio output is sent before the direct write call.
blocks.expected_output:
Hello from the C library
Hello from write

blocks.title: Output order and buffering
blocks.markdown: The order in which output appears can depend on buffering and whether streams are connected to a terminal or redirected. For a reliable tracing exercise, flush stdout or run the calls separately and inspect the system-call trace.

blocks.title: write(2) — Linux manual page
blocks.purpose: Read documented behaviour, return value and error conditions of the Linux write system call.

blocks.title: printf — The Open Group specification
blocks.purpose: Compare the standard formatted-output function with the lower-level write interface.

blocks.question: Why might a system-call tracing tool show write when a C program calls printf?
options: printf is itself a kernel system call.
The C library can format and buffer output, then call the operating-system write interface.
The compiler always replaces printf with assembly.
The kernel executes all C library functions.
blocks.explanation: printf is a C library function. The library may eventually use the operating-system write interface to send bytes to a file descriptor.

blocks.title: Observe the system-call boundary
blocks.objective: Compile a small C program and observe the operating-system calls involved in its output.
blocks.environment: Linux with a C compiler and strace. On macOS or Windows, use an appropriate platform tracing tool and adapt the commands.
instructions: Compile the example with warnings enabled.
Run it normally and note the output.
Run it under strace, filtering for write-related calls.
Compare the observed calls with the source code.
Repeat with output redirected to a file and note any buffering differences.
hints: If the trace is confusing, run the printf and write examples separately.
completion_criteria: Identify printf as a library function.
Identify write as a POSIX interface that reaches the kernel.
Explain why buffering affects when a write is observed.

lessons.title: Toolchain Fundamentals
lessons.subtitle: Verify the tools that turn source text into running bytes.
lessons.summary: Install and verify gcc, g++, nasm, gdb and python, and see exactly what each stage of compilation does.
learning_objectives: Verify gcc, g++, nasm, gdb and python are available and explain what each does.
Distinguish preprocessing, compilation, assembly and linking using gcc flags.
Use objdump and nm to inspect a built binary and explain sections.
prerequisites: From a C Library Call to a System Call

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.markdown: You cannot debug what you cannot build. Every later module assumes you can go from `hello.c` → `a.exe` → `objdump` without guessing.

A C program does not jump directly to machine code. `gcc -E` shows preprocessor output (headers expanded, macros applied). `gcc -S` emits assembly text. `as` assembles to an object file (`.o` with machine bytes plus relocations). `ld` links objects and libraries into an executable with resolved addresses.

Run each flag once on the same `hello.c` — once you see the intermediate files, the pipeline stops being magic.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing source file going through preprocessor, compiler, assembler and linker to executable.
blocks.caption: The classical compilation pipeline. Each arrow is a gcc flag you can run yourself.
blocks.attribution: SysProgs original — based on classical Unix toolchain

blocks.explanation: Run each version check. On Windows with UCRT64 via MSYS2, gcc should report 12+; with the older mingw32 bundled, 6.3 is enough for modules 00-03 but upgrade for 04+.

blocks.title: Windows note
blocks.markdown: Use UCRT64 (not mingw32) for C++ 17/20, newer GDB, and consistent POSIX shims. `pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gdb nasm python` keeps the whole curriculum working.

blocks.explanation: Minimal hosted C program. It links against the C library by default; use -nostdlib later in assembly modules to avoid it.
blocks.build_command: gcc -E hello.c -o hello.i && wc -l hello.i; gcc -S hello.c -o hello.s && head -20 hello.s; gcc -c hello.c -o hello.o && nm hello.o | head
blocks.expected_output: hello.i has ~800 lines after headers; hello.s shows mov, call, ret; hello.o has T main

blocks.title: Binutils — objdump and nm
blocks.purpose: Learn to inspect sections, symbols and disassembly of object files.

blocks.question: What does gcc -S do without linking?
options: Preprocesses only and stops.
Emits assembly text and stops.
Assembles to machine code object (.o) and stops.
Links into a final executable.
blocks.explanation: -E stops after preprocessing, -S after compilation to assembly, -c after assembling to an object. Linking is the final ld step.

blocks.title: Trace the build
blocks.objective: Produce and inspect all intermediate artefacts of a single C file.
blocks.environment: Any OS with gcc, binutils (objdump/nm) and a text editor.
instructions: Create hello.c as above.
Run gcc -E, -S, -c and a final link, keeping every output file.
Compare wc -l of hello.i before and after adding #include <stdio.h>.
Run objdump -d hello.o and find main's assembly.
Run nm hello.o and identify which symbol is global (T) vs undefined (U).
hints: Use gcc -v hello.c to see the sub-commands gcc actually invokes.
completion_criteria: You have hello.i, hello.s, hello.o and hello.exe
You can explain which file each flag produced and why headers bloat hello.i

lessons.title: Memory Hierarchy and Locality
lessons.subtitle: Why sequential access wins and how 64 bytes shapes your code.
lessons.summary: Walk from registers to SSD, learn the 64-byte cache line, and measure why stride matters.
learning_objectives: Describe the hierarchy from registers → L1 → L2 → L3 → RAM → SSD with latency intuition.
Explain the 64-byte cache line and why sequential access is faster per byte.
Predict cache-line and TLB effects and name fixes like alignas(64) and huge pages.
prerequisites: Basic C and ability to compile hello.c

blocks.title: The key idea
blocks.markdown: The CPU never sees RAM directly. It sees registers (1 cycle), then caches that hide RAM's ~80 ns latency. A line is **64 bytes** — fetch one byte and you fetch 63 neighbours. Algorithms that respect this win by 10×.

Registers live on the core itself — tens of bytes, 1 cycle. L1 (32 KiB, ~4 cycles) and L2 (256 KiB, ~12 cycles) are per-core; L3 (8–32 MiB, ~40 cycles) is shared. Main memory is gigabytes at ~80 ns plus 4 KiB pages via the TLB. Storage (NVMe/SSD) is milliseconds-away by comparison. The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches virtual→physical page mappings; a TLB miss triggers a page walk (four memory reads on x64).

Programs that miss often do not wait for one miss — they wait for many. Good layout turns misses into hits.

blocks.alt: Interactive diagram of the memory hierarchy from registers through L1, L2, L3, RAM with TLB and SSD.
blocks.caption: Hover any box for latency/size. Click for detail. Ctrl+wheel to zoom — uses the same interactive helper as the Study app.

blocks.explanation: Stride 1 touches every byte of each 64-byte line. Stride 16 (64 bytes) touches one int per line and wastes 60 bytes. Report time per element to see the per-line cost.
blocks.expected_output: seq 0.04s stride16 0.02s — but per element stride 16 is slower after normalising by elements touched

blocks.title: Numbers are approximate
blocks.markdown: L1 4c / RAM 80 ns / SSD 50 µs figures vary by chip and configuration. Use them as intuition, not datasheet. Measure on your machine with bench/cache-stride.c and note your own ratios.

blocks.title: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory (Ulrich Drepper)
blocks.purpose: Deeper reference for caches, VM, TLB and NUMA. Skim section 2–3 for this lesson.

blocks.question: Why is sequential array traversal usually faster per byte than strided traversal that skips 60 bytes each step?
options: The CPU has a special sequential instruction.
Each miss fetches a 64-byte line; sequential touches every byte of the line, strided wastes most of it.
Sequential uses fewer registers.
Strided uses more power and throttles.
blocks.explanation: A cache miss loads a full 64-byte line. Sequential uses the whole line before the next miss; strided loads a line for 4 bytes and discards 60.

blocks.title: See the line size yourself
blocks.objective: Observe cache-line effects by varying stride and interpreting timing.
blocks.environment: C compiler with -O2; any desktop OS.
instructions: Compile and run cache-stride.c with -O2 and note both timings.
Divide each timing by number of elements visited to get per-element cost.
Change N to 1K and re-measure — does the advantage remain?
Look up your L1 size (32 KiB vs 48 KiB) and explain when the array stops fitting.
hints: Keep s volatile so the compiler does not optimise away the loop.
Try stride 8 (32 bytes) vs 16 (64 bytes) vs 32 (128 bytes) and plot.
completion_criteria: You report seq vs strided per-element cost
You explain why per-element cost rises at 64-byte stride
You note where L1/L2 would fit the working set

lessons.title: Endianness and Alignment
lessons.subtitle: How bytes sit in memory — and why struct {char; int;} is not 5 bytes.
lessons.summary: See little vs big endian, network order, and the padding rules that decide struct layout and size.
learning_objectives: Predict memory byte order for a 32-bit integer on little vs big endian.
Use htonl/ntohl correctly and explain why networking needs it.
Explain why padding exists, compute sizeof and offsetof, and fix layout with reordering or alignas.

blocks.title: Memory is just bytes
blocks.markdown: A `uint32_t 0x01020304` is four bytes. The machine must pick an order to store them. Your laptop (x64, ARM default) picks little-endian: `04 03 02 01` in RAM. The network picks big-endian: `01 02 03 04` on the wire. Every `struct` is this idea plus alignment.

Write a 4-byte value, dump it with a hex tool or by casting to bytes. The order you see in RAM is the machine's endianness. The value as an integer is the same; the bytes in memory are reversed between the two conventions.

Networking code always converts with `htonl` / `ntohl` so peers agree. Skipping the call is the classic bug that works on one machine and fails on another.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing 0x01020304 stored as 01 02 03 04 on big-endian and 04 03 02 01 on little-endian.
blocks.caption: Same value, different byte order in memory. Network order is big-endian by definition.

blocks.explanation: Casts the integer's address to bytes and prints them. On little-endian you see 04 03 02 01; swap the bytes and print again to show the conversion.

blocks.markdown:
CPUs prefer aligned access: a 4-byte `int` wants address % 4 == 0, an 8-byte pointer wants % 8. The compiler inserts unnamed padding bytes so every member is aligned. `struct { char a; int b; }` has 1 byte for `a`, 3 bytes of padding, then 4 bytes for `b` → 8 bytes total. Put the big member first and you save the padding.

`sizeof` includes padding. `offsetof` tells you where each member sits. `alignas` forces a stricter alignment (for example 64 to avoid false sharing on a cache line).

blocks.explanation: Prints size, padding and offset. Swapping member order shows how layout affects size. Visualise with web/assets diagrams or your own drawings.
blocks.expected_output: A 8 ... B 8 (but packing differs; try char; char; int etc.)

blocks.title: C language — offsetof and alignas
blocks.purpose: Check padding, alignment and offsetof guarantees before trusting folklore.

blocks.question: On a little-endian machine, struct {char a; int b;} with a=0x11, b=0x01020304 will most likely occupy how many bytes and what byte sequence starts the struct?
blocks.explanation: Padding inserts 3 bytes after a so that b starts at an aligned offset. b itself is stored little-endian: 04 03 02 01.

blocks.title: Shrink a struct
blocks.objective: Reorder members and measure sizeof / offsetof.
instructions: Create struct D with members char, double, char, int.
Predict sizeof(D) before running.
Print sizeof and offsetof for each member.
Reorder members by descending alignment (double → int → char) and re-measure.
Try __attribute__((packed)) or #pragma pack(1) and reason why production code rarely uses them.
hints: double wants 8-byte alignment; char wants 1. Sorting biggest first minimises holes.
completion_criteria: You report original and reordered sizes with an explanation
You state where padding bytes sit

lessons.title: Stack Frames, Calls and ABIs
lessons.subtitle: The universal shape that every language lowers to.
lessons.summary: Draw the x64 stack frame, learn SysV vs Win64 calling, and read objdump like prose.
learning_objectives: Draw a stack frame (high→low, return address, saved rbp, locals, 16-byte align).
Map a C function call to push/call/mov/sub/ret and explain callee vs caller saved registers.
Distinguish SysV AMD64, Win64, AAPCS64 and RISC-V calling conventions and their pitfalls.
prerequisites: Ability to run gcc -S and objdump

blocks.title: One picture to memorize
blocks.markdown: Every compiled language lowers calls to the same shape: caller pushes a return address, callee sets up a frame (`push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; sub rsp,N`), uses locals, tears down, and `ret` pops the address back. Get this picture and GDB backtraces stop being mysterious.

`call foo` pushes `RIP` (8 bytes) so the CPU knows where to return, then jumps. Inside `foo`, `push rbp` saves the caller's frame pointer, `mov rbp,rsp` makes the new base, `sub rsp,16` reserves locals while keeping 16-byte alignment for the next `call`. The debugger walks `saved rbp` links to show a backtrace. Forgetting the 16-byte rule makes `movaps` in the callee fault with #GP — a classic hand-written-assembly bug.

SysV leaf functions may use 128 bytes *below* `RSP` without adjusting `RSP` (red zone). Win64 requires 32 bytes of *shadow space* above the return address for the callee to spill registers — reserve it even if you don't use it.

blocks.alt: Interactive stack frame diagram showing high to low memory: arguments, return address, saved rbp, locals, alignment.
blocks.caption: Interactive — hover each box for what call/push/sub does. Click for ABI detail. Ctrl+wheel to zoom.

blocks.source:
; caller
call foo        ; push RIP (rsp-=8, [rsp]=ret), jmp foo
; foo prologue
push rbp
mov  rbp, rsp
sub  rsp, 16      ; locals, keep 16B align
mov  [rbp-8], rdi ; spill arg
; ... body ...
add  rsp, 16
pop  rbp
ret              ; pop RIP -> jmp back
blocks.explanation: Annotated x64 prologue/epilogue. High address at top, RSP grows down. RBP is the debugger's bookmark.

blocks.markdown: Calling conventions decide register ownership. SysV AMD64 callee must preserve `rbx, rbp, r12-r15`; Win64 preserves `rbx, rbp, rsi, rdi, r12-r15`; AAPCS64 preserves `x19-x28, SP`. Everything else is caller-clobbered. Clobbering a callee-saved register without restoring it corrupts the caller's data *after* the call returns — the bug appears one frame up, not inside the function you wrote.

blocks.alt: Table comparing SysV AMD64, Win64, AAPCS64 and RISC-V register arguments and preserved registers.
blocks.caption: System V vs Win64 vs AAPCS64 vs RISC-V. rdi/rsi/rdx etc. map to x0-x7 / a0-a7.

blocks.source:
cc -O0 -g add.c -c -o add.o
objdump -d add.o | less
cc -O2 add.c -S -o add.s && cat add.s
# try godbolt.org for ARM/RISC-V cross views
blocks.explanation: Build with and without optimisation; compare how -O2 removes the frame or inlines. Use Compiler Explorer for A64 (aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc) and RV64.
blocks.build_command: cc -O0 -g -c example.c -o example.o && objdump -d example.o | head -40

blocks.title: System V AMD64 ABI (x86-64 psABI)
blocks.purpose: Authoritative callee/caller saved, red zone, and argument registers.

blocks.title: x64 calling conventions — Win64 vs SysV
blocks.purpose: Contrast shadow space and preserved registers.

blocks.question: A leaf function under SysV uses [rsp-8] without sub rsp,8 and never calls another function. What allows this?
options: The compiler always pads stacks by 8.
The 128-byte red zone below RSP that leaf functions may use without adjusting RSP.
Win64 shadow space guarantees 32 bytes.
GDB injects hidden padding.
blocks.explanation: SysV defines a 128-byte red zone below RSP for leaf functions. Win64 has a different concept: 32-byte shadow space above the return address for spilling.

blocks.title: Read your own frame
blocks.objective: Write a C function, compile to assembly and map every instruction to the frame picture.
instructions: Write int add(int a,int b){ return a+b; } and int main that calls it.
Compile with -O0 -g and -O2 separately, dump with gcc -S and objdump -d.
Annotate where arguments arrive (rdi/rsi on SysV) and where the return leaves (rax).
Introduce a local array char buf[16]; observe sub rsp alignment.
Break with gdb, run bt and info reg rbp/rsp.
completion_criteria: You can draw your add's frame with addresses and register values
You state which registers are caller vs callee saved for your toolchain

lessons.title: Pointers, Arrays and Memory Lifetime
lessons.subtitle: Make decay, lifetime and ownership visible — before you allocate.
lessons.summary: Distinguish arrays vs pointers, stack vs heap, and manage allocation with a disciplined mental model.
learning_objectives: Explain array decay and why sizeof(arr) differs in caller vs callee.
Describe stack, static and heap lifetime and when each is appropriate.
Implement and reason about malloc/free discipline without leaks or use-after-free.

blocks.title: C's sharp edge
blocks.markdown: In C, you manage every byte's lifetime. The compiler will not free for you, will not bounds-check, and will not warn about every use-after-free. The mental model — decay, lifetime, ownership — must be yours.

`int a[4]` is four ints laid out contiguously. `sizeof(a)` is the whole array (16 bytes on most platforms). When you pass `a` to a function, it *decays* to `int*` — a pointer to the first element — and `sizeof` inside the callee now measures the pointer (8 bytes). `a[2]` is just `*(a+2)`. `char *s` may point to read-only literal storage; `char s[]` makes a writable copy on the stack. Confusing these is the most common C beginner bug after off-by-one.

blocks.explanation: Prints sizes to show decay. Also shows literal vs array storage.
blocks.expected_output: in main: 16 vs pointer 8\nin f: 8\nlit pointer 8 arr bytes 3

blocks.markdown: Stack holds automatic locals and call frames — fast, limited (commonly 1–8 MiB), gone on return. Static storage (globals, `static` locals) lives for the whole run. Heap (via `malloc`/`free`) persists until you free it — you decide, you fail. `mmap` / `VirtualAlloc` is the underlying page-level primitive; `malloc` layers bins, free lists and coalescing on top of it. A bump allocator is 40 lines: a pointer that only grows; freeing is a reset.

blocks.explanation: Archetypal arena allocator. No free of individual blocks, only reset. Real malloc adds free lists, reuse and coalescing — see modules/03-c/memory.

blocks.title: Ownership, not syntax
blocks.markdown: Decide at every allocation: who owns this pointer, when does it die, what happens on failure (`malloc` returns NULL). Write the free *before* the logic, or use a single exit path. Leaks and double-frees are ownership failures, not typos.

blocks.title: C11 Standard — Memory and object lifetime (draft)
blocks.purpose: First-class reference for lifetime, sizeof and pointer semantics.

blocks.title: AddressSanitizer and the sanitizers
blocks.purpose: Detect leaks, use-after-free and overflows at runtime — use ASan while you learn, not after.

blocks.question: Why does sizeof(a) differ inside main vs inside f(int a[4])?
options: The compiler optimises main differently.
Arrays decay to pointers when passed; sizeof in f measures a pointer.
a is copied by value and shrinks.
sizeof is implementation-defined and random.
blocks.explanation: Formal parameters declared as a[4] adjust to int*. sizeof of a pointer (8 on 64-bit) is not the size of the original array.

blocks.title: Find the leak before ASan does
blocks.objective: Write a heap routine with deliberate unsafety, then fix it and prove it with sanitizers.
blocks.environment: gcc or clang, any OS; -fsanitize=address for the check.
instructions: Write a function char* make_greeting(const char* name) that mallocs, sprintfs and returns.
Call it in a loop 1000 times without free — observe growth with top / Task Manager.
Run with cc -fsanitize=address -g and read the report when you free incorrectly or use-after-free.
Fix: free after every call and set pointer to NULL after freeing.
Port the 40-line bump allocator to a free-list allocator sketch and keep ownership notes.
hints: ASan + UBSan together: -fsanitize=address,undefined. LeakSanitizer runs at exit.
completion_criteria: You can run under ASan with zero reports
You can describe each pointer's lifetime in one sentence
